entries.name: Coyote time
entries.summary: For a short moment after the player runs off a ledge, jump still works as if they were on the ground.
entries.what_it_does: Players press jump a few frames late all the time, mostly right at the edge of a platform. Without coyote time the game sees that press as "in the air" and ignores it, and the player falls while sure they pressed jump. With it, you track how long ago the player last stood on ground and allow a normal jump while that time is under the window.
entries.use_when: Any platformer with gaps or ledges.
entries.watch_out: Never give it after a jump has already started, or it turns into a free double jump.
entries.starting_values: Around 100 ms is a common starting point. Celeste's public player code uses a 0.1 second jump grace time. Try 60 to 150 ms.
entries.prompt:
Add coyote time to the player's jump.
- Track the time since the player was last on the ground.
- Allow a normal ground jump while that time is under 100 ms, even if the player is no longer touching the ground.
- Only after walking off an edge. Once any jump starts, clear the timer so coyote time can't give a second jump.
- Put the window in a named constant (COYOTE_MS = 100) and use real time (delta time), not frame counts.

Acceptance checks:
1. Walking off an edge and pressing jump 50 ms later jumps.
2. Pressing jump 150 ms after leaving the edge does nothing.
3. Jumping, then pressing jump again in the air, never gives a second jump.

entries.name: Jump buffering
entries.summary: If the player presses jump just before landing, remember the press for a short time and jump the moment they touch the ground.
entries.what_it_does: When players chain jumps they often press a little early, while still falling. Without a buffer that press is thrown away because they weren't on the ground yet, and the game feels like it ignored them. With a buffer you store when jump was pressed, and on each frame you jump if the player is grounded and the press is recent enough.
entries.use_when: Any game with repeated jumps, and the same idea works for dashes and other moves.
entries.watch_out: Keep the window short. A long buffer makes the character jump when the player has already changed their mind.
entries.starting_values: 100 to 150 ms is a common start. Celeste's player code reads jump from a buffered input and consumes the buffer when a jump starts.
entries.prompt:
Add jump buffering.
- When jump is pressed, store the time of the press.
- Every frame, if the player is grounded and a jump press happened in the last 120 ms, jump and clear the stored press.
- Only new presses count. Holding the button must not auto-repeat jumps.
- Use real time (delta time) for the window. JUMP_BUFFER_MS = 120.

Acceptance checks:
1. Pressing jump 60 ms before landing jumps on the frame the player lands.
2. Pressing jump 170 ms before landing does nothing.
3. Holding jump through a landing does not trigger a second jump.

entries.name: Variable jump height
entries.summary: Tap jump for a short hop, hold it for a full jump. When the player lets go while still rising, cut the upward speed.
entries.what_it_does: With one fixed jump, small hops are impossible and the player spends a long time in the air for every tiny step, which reads as floaty. The common fix: when jump is released and the character is still moving up, multiply the vertical speed by a number under 1. Gravity then ends the jump sooner.
entries.use_when: Platformers where the player needs both small and big jumps.
entries.watch_out: Games where every jump should be identical on purpose, like some puzzle or rhythm games.
entries.starting_values: A cut of 0.4 to 0.5 is a common start. Celeste does it differently: it keeps the jump speed for up to 0.2 seconds while the button is held. Both work.
entries.prompt:
Add variable jump height.
- Jump starts with an upward speed of 480 px/s.
- When the jump button is released while the player is still moving up, multiply vertical speed by 0.45.
- Apply the cut only once per jump and only while rising.

Acceptance checks:
1. A quick tap peaks clearly lower than a full hold. Log both peak heights.
2. Releasing the button while falling changes nothing.
3. A full hold reaches the same height as before this change.

entries.name: Camera lookahead and smoothing
entries.summary: The camera aims a bit ahead of where the player is facing and eases toward that point instead of being glued to the player.
entries.what_it_does: A camera locked to the player's center shows as much level behind them as ahead. Lookahead shifts the target in the facing direction so the player sees what's coming. Smoothing moves the camera part of the way toward its target each frame, so turns and stops don't snap. Using 1 - exp(-speed * dt) keeps the smoothing the same at any frame rate.
entries.use_when: Side-scrollers and top-down games where the level is bigger than the screen.
entries.watch_out: Single-screen games. Too much smoothing on a fast character feels laggy.
entries.starting_values: Lookahead around 15 percent of the view width (about 90 px here). Smoothing speed 4 to 8 with exponential damping.
entries.prompt:
Make the camera follow with lookahead and smoothing.
- Keep a facing offset that eases toward facing * 90 px, so turning around pans instead of snapping.
- Camera target x = player center x + facing offset.
- Each frame: camera.x += (target - camera.x) * (1 - Math.exp(-6 * dt)), with dt in seconds.
- Clamp the camera to the level bounds.
- Shake and UI are separate layers. Lookahead only moves the world camera.

Acceptance checks:
1. Running right shows more level to the right of the player than to the left.
2. Turning around pans smoothly over roughly half a second, with no snap.
3. The camera does not jitter while the player stands still.
4. Locking the game to 30 fps and to 144 fps gives the same camera motion.

sources.title: Juicing Your Cameras With Math (Squirrel Eiserloh, GDC)

entries.name: Input buffering for attacks
entries.summary: A press made during an attack's recovery is saved and fires the moment the attack ends, instead of being thrown away.
entries.what_it_does: Players press the next attack before the current one finishes. If the game only accepts input when the character is idle, those presses vanish and combat feels sticky. A buffer keeps one press made near the end of recovery and starts the next attack on the first frame it's allowed.
entries.use_when: Melee combat, combos, fighting games, any move with recovery time.
entries.watch_out: Keep it to one queued press. Queueing every press makes the character keep swinging after the player stopped.
entries.starting_values: A buffer of 100 to 200 ms before recovery ends. Recovery itself of 150 to 300 ms for a light attack.
entries.prompt:
Add an input buffer for attacks.
- Each attack has an active phase and a recovery phase (220 ms).
- If attack is pressed while an attack is running and less than 150 ms of it remain, queue one press.
- When recovery ends and a press is queued, start the next attack on that frame.
- Earlier presses are ignored. Only one press can be queued.
- Show a debug counter of dropped presses.

Acceptance checks:
1. Pressing attack again 75 ms before recovery ends chains into a second attack with no idle frame.
2. Pressing attack at the very start of an attack does not queue anything.
3. Holding the button does not auto-attack.

entries.name: Invincibility frames with flicker
feels: lost all my health at once
entries.summary: After taking a hit, the player can't be hurt again for a short time, and the sprite flickers so they know.
entries.what_it_does: Without i-frames, touching a hazard deals damage every frame you overlap it, so one mistake empties the health bar. With them, a hit starts a timer and further damage is ignored until it runs out. Flickering the sprite shows the state without any extra UI.
entries.use_when: Anything with health and contact damage.
entries.watch_out: One-hit-death games, where the hit ends the attempt anyway.
entries.starting_values: 0.5 to 1.5 seconds for platformers. Flicker every 60 to 100 ms.
entries.prompt:
Add invincibility frames after the player takes damage.
- On damage, set invulnerableUntil = now + 1000 ms. Ignore damage while now < invulnerableUntil.
- While invulnerable, draw the sprite only when Math.floor(now / 80) % 2 === 0.
- Movement, input and hitboxes keep working during the flicker.
- Use time, not frame counts.

Acceptance checks:
1. Standing inside a hazard takes one hit per 1000 ms, not one per frame.
2. The sprite is fully visible again when the window ends.
3. Flicker speed is the same at 30 and 144 fps.

entries.name: Hitstop
entries.summary: Freeze the action for a few frames when a hit lands so the impact registers.
entries.what_it_does: When a hit connects and everything keeps moving, the eye barely registers contact. A short freeze on the hit frame gives it weight. Too long and the game feels like it's stuttering.
entries.use_when: Melee hits, heavy impacts, parries, the last hit of a combo.
entries.watch_out: Rapid-fire weapons that hit many times a second, where freezes would stack into lag.
entries.starting_values: 50 to 100 ms (3 to 6 frames at 60 fps) for normal hits, longer for heavy ones. Celeste's player code freezes the game for 0.05 seconds on some actions.
entries.prompt:
Add hitstop when an attack connects.
- On hit, set hitstopRemaining = max(hitstopRemaining, 80 ms). Don't add freezes together.
- While hitstopRemaining > 0, skip gameplay updates (movement, physics, animation timers) but keep reading input and keep audio playing.
- Count down in real time.
- Presses made during the freeze still take effect after it.

Acceptance checks:
1. One hit freezes the action for about 80 ms.
2. Ten quick hits never produce one long freeze.
3. A jump pressed during the freeze happens right after it.

entries.name: Screen shake with falloff
entries.summary: Shake the camera on impact, with the strength fading over time instead of a constant jitter.
entries.what_it_does: Each impact adds trauma, a number from 0 to 1. Shake strength is trauma squared, so small hits barely move the view and big ones hit hard, and trauma falls back to 0 at a steady rate. That approach comes from Squirrel Eiserloh's GDC talk. Use smooth noise rather than a new random offset each frame, shake only the world camera and never the UI, and give players a way to turn it off.
entries.use_when: Explosions, heavy hits, landing from a big fall.
entries.watch_out: Every small event. Constant shake is tiring, and some players get motion sick.
entries.starting_values: Max offset 15 to 25 px at this 640 px view (one hit at 0.5 trauma moves about a quarter of that), falloff 1.5 to 2.5 trauma per second.
entries.prompt:
Add screen shake with falloff using a trauma value.
- trauma is 0 to 1. Each hit adds 0.5 (clamped to 1). trauma decreases by 1.8 per second.
- Each frame: shake = 20 px * trauma * trauma. Offset the world camera by shake times smooth noise (sum of two sine waves or Perlin noise), not a new random number per frame.
- Apply it only to the world camera. HUD and menus never shake.
- Add a settings toggle to turn shake off, and default it to off when prefers-reduced-motion is set.

Acceptance checks:
1. One hit gives a visible shake that settles within about 0.3 second(s).
2. Several quick hits shake harder but never past 20 px.
3. HUD text stays still while the world shakes.
4. With the setting off, nothing moves.

entries.name: Acceleration and deceleration
entries.summary: Speed ramps up to max and back down to zero over a short time instead of snapping. The balance between the two decides whether movement feels tight or slippery.
entries.what_it_does: Instant velocity (full speed on the first frame, zero the frame you let go) feels robotic. Low deceleration feels like ice. Most platformers reach top speed in a fraction of a second and stop a little faster or slower depending on the feel they want. Use a separate, usually smaller, multiplier in the air.
entries.use_when: Almost any character controller.
entries.watch_out: Grid-based or tile-step movement, where position snaps on purpose.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code uses a max run of 90 and run acceleration of 1000 (pixels per second at 320 by 180), so it reaches full speed in under a tenth of a second. This demo is twice that resolution: max 200 px/s, acceleration 2000, deceleration 1600.
entries.prompt:
Replace instant horizontal movement with acceleration and deceleration.
- Max speed 200 px/s.
- While input is held in the direction of motion, move velocity toward max speed by 2000 px/s² * dt.
- With no input, or input against the motion, move velocity toward 0 (or toward the new direction) by 1600 px/s² * dt.
- In the air, multiply both by 0.7.
- Use a move-toward function so velocity never overshoots the target.

Acceptance checks:
1. From standing, full speed takes about 100 ms.
2. Releasing at full speed stops the character within a short, consistent distance.
3. Turning around never flips speed instantly.
4. Behavior is the same at 30 and 144 fps.

entries.name: Knockback
entries.summary: A hit pushes the target away from the attacker with a small upward pop, then friction slows it down.
entries.what_it_does: If a target doesn't react to being hit, it reads as if the attack missed. Knockback sets the target's velocity away from the attacker on the hit frame and lets friction bring it to a stop. It pairs well with hitstop: freeze first, then launch.
entries.use_when: Melee and projectile hits, explosions, and also the player getting hit.
entries.watch_out: Puzzle games where position must stay exact, or near walls and pits unless you want that to be part of the game.
entries.starting_values: Force 250 to 400 px/s with an upward pop around 40 to 50 percent of that, friction 1000 to 2000 px/s².
entries.prompt:
Add knockback when an attack hits an enemy.
- On hit: enemy.vx = attackerFacing * 340 px/s, enemy.vy = -340 * 0.45.
- While the enemy is on the ground, move vx toward 0 by 1400 px/s² * dt.
- The enemy can't act until it stops sliding (hitstun).
- If hitstop is in the game, apply knockback after the freeze ends.

Acceptance checks:
1. A hit always pushes the enemy away from the attacker, from both sides.
2. The slide distance is the same at 30 and 144 fps.
3. Knockback into a wall stops cleanly with no clipping into it.

entries.name: Apex hang
entries.summary: Near the top of a jump, while jump is held, gravity is cut so the player hangs for a moment and can line up the landing.
entries.what_it_does: A plain jump spends very little time near its peak, and that is exactly where players aim. Apex hang checks how fast the character is moving vertically. When that speed is small (the character is near the top) and the jump button is still held, gravity is multiplied by a number under 1. The jump gets a short float at the top while the rise and the fall stay the same.
entries.use_when: Platformers with precise landings, especially on small platforms.
entries.watch_out: Too low a multiplier or too wide a band makes every jump float. Only apply it while the button is held, so a tap still drops fast.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code halves gravity (0.5) when vertical speed is under 40 and jump is held. That is 40 px/s at Celeste's 320 by 180, about 80 px/s at this demo's 640 by 360.
entries.prompt:
Add apex hang to the jump.
- While the player is in the air, jump is held, and the absolute vertical speed is under 80 px/s, multiply gravity by 0.5.
- Everywhere else, gravity is normal.
- Keep the takeoff speed and the max fall speed unchanged.

Acceptance checks:
1. A held jump stays in the air longer than before. Log the air time both ways.
2. A tapped jump (released early) gets no float.
3. Outside the top band, the rise and the fall match the old jump.

entries.name: Heavier fall
entries.summary: Gravity gets stronger once the character starts falling, so jumps rise smoothly and come down fast.
entries.what_it_does: A real projectile arc is symmetric: the fall takes as long as the rise. In a game that often reads as floaty. Switching to a heavier gravity after the peak, when vertical speed turns downward, makes the fall quicker while the rise stays the same. The jump keeps its height but spends less time in the air. Kyle Pittman's GDC talk on jump math describes switching gravity at the peak.
entries.use_when: Any jump that feels floaty or slow to come down.
entries.watch_out: Raise the max fall speed with it, or the fall hits the cap quickly and the multiplier stops mattering. Very high values make drops hard to steer.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives one number. 1.5 to 2.5 times normal gravity is a sensible starting range to tune.
entries.prompt:
Make the jump fall faster than it rises.
- Keep normal gravity while vertical speed is upward.
- Once vertical speed is downward (after the peak), multiply gravity by 1.8.
- Keep the takeoff speed, so the peak height does not change.
- Keep the max fall speed high enough that the multiplier still matters.

Acceptance checks:
1. The peak height is the same as before.
2. Total air time is shorter than before. Log both.
3. Gravity on the way up is unchanged.

sources.title: Math for Game Programmers: Building a Better Jump (Kyle Pittman, GDC)

entries.name: Terminal velocity
entries.summary: Cap how fast the character can fall, so long drops stay readable and steerable.
entries.what_it_does: Gravity adds speed every frame. Without a cap, a long fall gets faster and faster until the player can't react to anything on the way down, and fast bodies can skip through thin obstacles. A max fall speed clamps vertical speed after gravity is added. Some games also let the player hold down to fall faster, up to a second, higher cap.
entries.use_when: Any game with gravity and falls longer than one jump.
entries.watch_out: A cap that is too low makes falling feel like gliding. Check collisions at the capped speed so nothing tunnels.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code caps falling at 160, or 240 while holding down, in pixels per second at 320 by 180. That is 320 and 480 px/s at this demo's size.
entries.prompt:
Cap the player's fall speed.
- After adding gravity each frame, clamp vertical speed to at most 320 px/s downward.
- Optional: while down is held, raise the cap gradually to about 1.5 times that.
- Upward speed is not capped by this.

Acceptance checks:
1. A long fall never goes faster than 320 px/s. Log the speed.
2. Short jumps feel the same as before.
3. At the capped speed the player never passes through a thin platform.

entries.name: Corner correction
entries.summary: When a jump clips the corner of a ceiling by a few pixels, slide the player sideways around it instead of stopping the jump.
entries.what_it_does: Players often jump up through a gap and catch its edge with the side of their head. Without help the jump stops dead and they fall. Corner correction checks, at the moment of the bump, whether moving the player a few pixels left or right would clear the ceiling. If it would, it moves them there and the jump continues.
entries.use_when: Platformers with narrow gaps, doorways or low ceilings.
entries.watch_out: Keep it to a few pixels. A large nudge visibly teleports the player and can carry them past walls you meant to block.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code checks up to 4 pixels each way when moving up (at 320 by 180), about 8 px at this demo's size. Game Maker's Toolkit's Celeste video mentions the same kind of corner forgiveness for dashes.
entries.prompt:
Add corner correction for upward movement.
- When the player is moving up and hits a ceiling, test shifting them sideways by 1 to 8 px.
- If a shifted position is free of solids, move the player there and keep the upward speed. Test toward the direction of horizontal movement, or both sides when not moving sideways.
- If no shift clears it, stop the jump as usual.

Acceptance checks:
1. Jumping into a gap while clipping its edge by 4 px passes through.
2. Jumping squarely into a ceiling still stops the jump.
3. The nudge never moves the player into a wall.

entries.name: Double jump
entries.summary: Allow one extra jump in the air, refilled when the player lands.
entries.what_it_does: A second jump lets players fix a jump that went wrong and reach higher places. Keep a counter of air jumps left, refill it on landing, and spend one when jump is pressed in the air. A coyote jump off a ledge should count as the ground jump, not use up the air jump.
entries.use_when: Games about exploration or recovery, where reaching higher spots is the reward.
entries.watch_out: Every gap and ledge now has to account for the extra height, which makes levels harder to design. Precise platformers often leave it out.
entries.starting_values: Rodrigo Monteiro's platformer guide describes the counter approach and notes that the second jump is sometimes shorter. 0.8 to 1.0 times the first jump's speed is a sensible starting range.
entries.prompt:
Add a double jump.
- Keep airJumpsLeft. Set it to 1 whenever the player is on the ground.
- When jump is pressed in the air, a normal or coyote jump is not allowed, and airJumpsLeft > 0: set vertical speed to 0.85 times the normal jump speed (upward) and decrease airJumpsLeft.
- Each press can do only one jump.

Acceptance checks:
1. Jump, then jump again in the air: the second jump works.
2. A third press in the air does nothing.
3. Landing refills the extra jump.

sources.title: The guide to implementing 2D platformers (Rodrigo Monteiro, Higher-Order Fun)

entries.name: Landing recovery
entries.summary: After a hard landing, the character can't act for a few frames, which gives falls weight.
entries.what_it_does: A character who can run at full speed the instant they hit the ground after a long fall feels weightless. Landing recovery locks movement and jumping for a short time after any landing faster than a threshold. Small hops stay free, so normal play is not slowed down. A squash on the landing frame shows the player why they are stuck.
entries.use_when: Games that want weight: brawlers, fighting games, heavy characters.
entries.watch_out: Precise platformers, where any lost control feels unfair. Keep it short and only on hard landings.
entries.starting_values: SmashWiki's landing lag page lists light landings at 2 frames and heavy landings from 2 to 6 frames in later Smash games, about 33 to 100 ms at 60 fps.
entries.prompt:
Add landing recovery after hard landings.
- On the frame the player lands, if their downward speed was at least 600 px/s, block movement and jumping for 100 ms (6 frames at 60 fps).
- Lighter landings get no recovery.
- Squash the sprite on the landing frame so the player sees why.

Acceptance checks:
1. Dropping from a high ledge stops the player for about 100 ms.
2. A normal hop on flat ground never triggers it.
3. The timing is the same at 30 and 144 fps.

sources.title: SmashWiki: Landing lag

entries.name: One-way platforms with drop-through
entries.summary: Platforms you can jump up through from below and land on from above, with down plus jump to drop back through.
entries.what_it_does: Solid platforms stop the player's head on the way up, so a stack of them becomes a maze. A one-way platform only blocks a body that was fully above its top edge before this frame's move and is moving down. Checking the previous position matters: a player who jumps halfway into the platform and falls back should drop through, not snap onto it. Dropping through ignores one-way platforms for a moment.
entries.use_when: Stacked platforms, multi-level arenas, anything the player should reach from below.
entries.watch_out: Keep the drop input distinct so it never fires by accident, for example down plus jump rather than down alone.
entries.starting_values: Rodrigo Monteiro's platformer guide gives the rule: the platform counts only if the player's bottom was above its top before the move. Ignoring one-way platforms for about 200 ms on a drop is a starting point to tune. Celeste's code has its own version, called JumpThru.
entries.prompt:
Add one-way platforms.
- They never block horizontal movement.
- They block vertical movement only when the player's bottom edge was at or above the platform's top before this frame's move, and the player is moving down.
- Drop-through: when the player stands on a one-way platform and presses down and jump together, ignore one-way platforms for 200 ms and do not jump.

Acceptance checks:
1. Jumping from below passes through and lands on top.
2. A jump that only reaches halfway through falls back down through it.
3. Down plus jump on a one-way platform drops through. On solid ground it does a normal jump.

entries.name: Air control
entries.summary: Let the player steer left and right during a jump, usually with weaker acceleration than on the ground.
entries.what_it_does: With no air control, the direction at takeoff decides the whole jump, which feels stiff and rules out small corrections. With air control, horizontal input keeps working in the air, using the ground acceleration times a multiplier. That multiplier sets how much the player can correct a jump once it has started.
entries.use_when: Nearly every platformer.
entries.watch_out: Games where committing to a jump is the point, like some cinematic platformers.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code multiplies run acceleration by 0.65 in the air. Game Maker's Toolkit points out that Madeline has so much air friction that she falls almost straight down when you let go of the stick.
entries.prompt:
Give the player air control.
- In the air, use the ground horizontal acceleration and deceleration multiplied by 0.65.
- Keep the same max speed in the air.
- Use delta time.

Acceptance checks:
1. Reversing direction in mid-air visibly bends the jump.
2. Letting go in the air slows horizontal speed at 0.65 times the ground rate.
3. Ground movement is unchanged.

entries.name: Turn-around speed
entries.summary: Give turning around its own, stronger acceleration so reversing is quick even when stopping is gentle.
entries.what_it_does: Many controllers use the stopping deceleration when the player reverses, so a soft stop also means a slow, skidding turn. Splitting the turn out gives one more knob: when input points against the current speed, use a separate, larger turn acceleration. The character keeps its gentle stop and still changes direction quickly.
entries.use_when: Characters that should feel nimble but not stop on a dime.
entries.watch_out: A heavy character with a deliberate skid wants the slow turn.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives a separate turn number. Game Maker's Toolkit notes that Madeline changes direction very quickly with no skidding, and Celeste's code uses its full run acceleration when turning. Try 2 to 3 times your normal acceleration.
entries.prompt:
Give turning its own acceleration.
- When horizontal input points opposite to the current horizontal speed, move speed toward the target at 4000 px/s² instead of the normal deceleration.
- Stopping with no input still uses the normal deceleration.
- Optional: spawn skid dust while turning.

Acceptance checks:
1. Reversing from full speed takes less time than before. Log both.
2. Releasing input still slides to a stop as before.
3. Same result at 30 and 144 fps.

entries.name: Wall slide
feels: can't line up a wall jump
entries.summary: Falling while pushing into a wall slows the fall, giving the player time to line up a wall jump.
entries.what_it_does: Without a slide, a player who reaches a wall falls past it at full speed and has a split second to react. A wall slide caps fall speed while the player is in the air, moving down, and holding toward a wall they touch. Celeste starts the cap very low and lets it rise back to normal fall speed over about a second, so nobody can hang forever.
entries.use_when: Games with wall jumps or vertical shafts.
entries.watch_out: Only slide while the player holds toward the wall, or they snag on every wall they brush past.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code starts the slide cap at 20 (40 px/s at this demo's size) and blends it back to the normal max fall speed over 1.2 seconds of sliding.
entries.prompt:
Add a wall slide.
- While in the air, moving down, and holding toward a wall the player touches: cap fall speed.
- The cap starts at 40 px/s and rises linearly to the normal max fall speed over 1200 ms of sliding.
- Reset the slide timer on landing or jumping.
- No slide when not holding toward the wall.

Acceptance checks:
1. Holding into a wall while falling slows the fall to about 40 px/s at first.
2. After 1200 ms of sliding, fall speed is back to normal.
3. Brushing past a wall without holding toward it does not slow the fall.

sources.title: Celeste player source (Player.cs), public on GitHub

entries.name: Wall jump input lockout
entries.summary: Right after a wall jump, ignore the direction input for a moment so the jump actually carries the player away from the wall.
entries.what_it_does: A wall jump pushes the player away from the wall. If they are still holding toward the wall, normal air control pulls them straight back, and they can climb a single wall by tapping jump. A short lockout forces the horizontal direction away from the wall for a few frames, then hands control back.
entries.use_when: Any game with wall jumps, unless climbing a single wall is meant to work.
entries.watch_out: Too long a lockout feels like the game took the controller away. Keep it short.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code forces the move direction for 0.16 seconds after a wall jump and pushes away at 130 (260 px/s at this demo's size). It accepts a wall up to 3 pixels away.
entries.prompt:
Add an input lockout after wall jumps.
- A wall jump sets vertical speed to the normal jump speed and horizontal speed to 260 px/s away from the wall.
- For 160 ms after the wall jump, ignore horizontal input and act as if the player is holding away from the wall.
- After that, normal air control returns.
- Allow the wall jump when a wall is within 3 px, not only when touching.

Acceptance checks:
1. Holding toward a single wall and tapping jump does not climb it.
2. Wall jumping back and forth between two walls still works.
3. Control returns 160 ms after the wall jump.

sources.title: Celeste player source (Player.cs), public on GitHub

entries.name: Dash with cooldown
entries.summary: A short burst of fixed speed in the facing direction, with a cooldown so it can't be chained into flying.
entries.what_it_does: A dash sets speed to a fixed value for a short time and ignores gravity. Without a limit, players chain dashes and skip the level. A cooldown blocks the next dash for a moment. Celeste also allows only one air dash until you land, which is a separate rule you can add on top.
entries.use_when: Action games that want a burst of speed or an escape move.
entries.watch_out: Show the cooldown with a meter or a color change, or players will think the game dropped their input.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code dashes at 240 (480 px/s at this demo's size) for 0.15 seconds, with a 0.2 second cooldown that starts when the dash begins. It also freezes the game for 0.05 seconds as a dash starts. This demo starts its cooldown when the dash ends.
entries.prompt:
Add a dash with a cooldown.
- On the dash button, if the dash is ready: set horizontal speed to facing * 480 px/s and vertical speed to 0 for 150 ms, with no gravity.
- When the dash ends, set horizontal speed to the normal max speed in the same direction.
- The next dash is allowed 200 ms after the previous one ends.
- Show readiness with a small meter or a color change.

Acceptance checks:
1. Mashing dash gives at most one dash per 150 + 200 ms.
2. A press during the cooldown does nothing, and the meter shows why.
3. Dash distance is the same at 30 and 144 fps.

sources.title: Celeste player source (Player.cs), public on GitHub

entries.name: Ledge grab
entries.summary: When a jump ends with the player's head level with a ledge they are pushing into, they catch it and hang, then jump to climb up.
entries.what_it_does: Players judge height badly, and missing a ledge by a few pixels is a common frustration. A ledge grab checks, while falling and holding toward a wall, whether the top corner of that wall is near the player's head. If it is, the player snaps to hang there. Jump climbs up, down lets go. A near miss becomes a success without making every jump higher.
entries.use_when: Adventure and action platformers, especially with realistic jump heights.
entries.watch_out: Precision platformers where exact jump height is the challenge. Block a new grab for a moment after letting go, or the player grabs again at once.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives numbers. A grab zone from about 10 px above to 8 px below the top of the head, and 300 ms before another grab after dropping, are starting points to tune.
entries.prompt:
Add a ledge grab.
- While in the air, falling, and holding toward a wall the player touches: if the top of that wall is between 10 px above and 8 px below the top of the player's head, snap the player to hang with their head just above the ledge. Set speed to 0 and stop gravity.
- While hanging: jump climbs up with a normal jump, down lets go.
- After letting go, don't allow another grab for 300 ms.

Acceptance checks:
1. A jump that ends just below a ledge catches it.
2. Pressing jump while hanging ends with the player standing on top.
3. Pressing down drops the player, who does not grab again right away.

entries.name: Slope snapping
entries.summary: When running downhill, keep the character on the slope instead of letting them skip down it in small hops.
entries.what_it_does: Running down a slope moves the character sideways faster than gravity pulls them down, so they leave the ground for a few frames, land, and leave again. They bounce, and jump presses fail while they are airborne. Slope snapping checks, after moving, whether the character was grounded last frame and the slope is only a few pixels below their feet. If so, it moves them down onto it.
entries.use_when: Any game with slopes or uneven ground.
entries.watch_out: Never snap right after a jump or over a real drop. Limit it to a few pixels, and only when the player was grounded last frame.
entries.starting_values: Rodrigo Monteiro's platformer guide explains the bouncing and two fixes: make gravity's minimum step match the slope, or keep the distance to the floor the same before and after moving. A snap distance of 8 to 16 px here is a starting point.
entries.prompt:
Keep the player attached to slopes when moving downhill.
- After movement: if the player was on the ground last frame, is not moving up, and the floor under their feet is between 0 and 12 px below them, move them down onto the floor and keep them grounded.
- Don't snap after a jump starts or when the gap is bigger than 12 px.

Acceptance checks:
1. Running down the slope at full speed keeps the player grounded every frame. Log airborne frames.
2. Jumping works at any point on the slope.
3. Running off a real ledge still falls normally.

sources.title: The guide to implementing 2D platformers (Rodrigo Monteiro, Higher-Order Fun)

entries.name: Moving platforms that carry the player
entries.summary: A player standing on a moving platform moves with it, and a jump off it keeps the platform's speed.
entries.what_it_does: If a moving platform is only a solid box, it slides out from under the player, who has to walk to keep up. The fix: before moving characters, find who stands on each platform, move the platform, then move those riders by the same amount. Celeste also adds the platform's speed to the player's when they jump off (its code calls this lift boost), so a jump from a fast platform carries.
entries.use_when: Any moving solid the player can stand on: lifts, carts, conveyor parts.
entries.watch_out: Cap the inherited speed so a fast platform can't fling the player across the level.
entries.starting_values: Rodrigo Monteiro's platformer guide gives the order: find riders, step platforms, shift riders by the platform's movement, then step characters. Celeste's public player code caps the inherited speed at 250 sideways and 130 upward (at 320 by 180).
entries.prompt:
Make moving platforms carry the player.
- Each frame, before moving the player, check whether they stand on a moving platform (bottom edge within 0.5 px of its top, overlapping horizontally).
- Move the platforms, then move each rider by the platform's change in position.
- When the player jumps off, add the platform's velocity to theirs, capped to a sensible max.
- In this demo the platform makes one round trip every 4 s.

Acceptance checks:
1. Standing still on a moving platform keeps the player on it.
2. Jumping off a moving platform carries its speed for a moment.
3. Walking on the platform works in both directions.

entries.name: Analog stick dead zone
entries.summary: Ignore tiny stick readings near the center, then rescale the rest so movement still starts smoothly from zero.
entries.what_it_does: Analog sticks rarely rest at exactly zero. Worn or loose sticks report a small value when nobody touches them, and the character creeps. A dead zone treats readings under a threshold as zero. Rescaling the rest of the range back to 0 to 1 avoids a jump in speed at the edge of the dead zone. This demo simulates a drifting stick with the keyboard: the arrow keys push a virtual stick that has some drift built in.
entries.use_when: Any game that reads analog sticks or triggers.
entries.watch_out: Too large a dead zone makes small, precise moves impossible. Test with a real controller.
entries.starting_values: Josh Sutphin's article on dead zones puts the usual threshold between 0.1 and 0.2 and recommends a scaled radial dead zone for 2D stick input.
entries.prompt:
Add a dead zone to analog stick input.
- Read the stick as a 2D vector. If its length is under 0.2, treat it as zero.
- Otherwise rescale: direction * (length - 0.2) / (1 - 0.2), so output starts at 0 at the dead zone edge and reaches 1 at full tilt.
- Apply it to the vector, not to each axis separately, so diagonals stay smooth.
- Make the threshold a setting.

Acceptance checks:
1. A resting stick with drift under the threshold moves nothing.
2. Pushing just past the dead zone gives a small speed, not a jump.
3. Full tilt still reaches full speed.

sources.title: Doing Thumbstick Dead Zones Right (Josh Sutphin, archived copy)

entries.name: Attack startup, active and recovery
entries.summary: Split each attack into a wind-up, a short window where it can hit, and a follow-through where the attacker is open.
entries.what_it_does: An attack that hits on the frame you press it and can be repeated at once has no weight and no risk. Fighting games split every move into startup (before it can hit), active (when the hitbox is out) and recovery (after, when the attacker can't act). Startup makes timing matter and recovery makes a miss costly. The active part is usually very short.
entries.use_when: Melee combat where timing and commitment should matter.
entries.watch_out: Long startup on a basic attack feels unresponsive. Keep light attacks quick, and buffer presses made during recovery.
entries.starting_values: Infil's fighting game glossary notes most moves have only about 1 to 4 active frames. This demo starts at 100 ms of startup (6 frames), 50 ms active (3 frames) and 250 ms of recovery (15 frames) as starting points to tune.
entries.prompt:
Give each attack three phases.
- Startup: 100 ms (6 frames) after the press, with no hitbox. Show a wind-up.
- Active: about 50 ms (3 frames) with the hitbox out. Each attack can hit a target once.
- Recovery: 250 ms (15 frames) with no hitbox, and the attacker can't start another attack.
- Store the phase timings per attack as data.

Acceptance checks:
1. A hit lands 6 frames after the press, not on the press.
2. Pressing attack during recovery does not start a new attack, unless a buffer or cancel rule allows it.
3. Phase lengths are the same at 30 and 144 fps.

sources.title: Infil's Fighting Game Glossary: Startup
Infil's Fighting Game Glossary: Active
Infil's Fighting Game Glossary: Recovery

entries.name: Cancel windows
entries.summary: After an attack connects, a short window lets the next attack start right away, skipping the rest of the recovery.
entries.what_it_does: Long recovery makes a missed attack risky, which is good, but it also makes landed hits slow to follow up. A cancel window opens only when the attack hit something: a press inside it starts the next attack at once. Misses keep the full recovery, so landing hits is rewarded and swinging at nothing is not.
entries.use_when: Combo-based combat, fighting games, character action games.
entries.watch_out: Too wide a window lets mashing do everything. Keep it to the moment right after a hit.
entries.starting_values: Infil's fighting game glossary defines a cancel as removing an attack's recovery to go straight into another move, usually after it hits. This demo uses a 150 ms window inside 300 ms of recovery as a starting point.
entries.prompt:
Add cancel windows to attacks.
- When an attack hits, open a cancel window for the first 150 ms of its recovery.
- Pressing attack inside the window starts the next attack immediately.
- If the attack missed, there is no window and the full recovery plays.
- Track a combo counter that resets after 600 ms without a hit.

Acceptance checks:
1. Hit, then press attack within 150 ms: the next attack starts on that frame.
2. A missed attack can't be cancelled.
3. A press outside the window does nothing until recovery ends.

sources.title: Infil's Fighting Game Glossary: Cancel
Infil's Fighting Game Glossary: Hit Confirm

entries.name: Dodge roll
entries.summary: A quick roll that can't be hurt for its length, so a well-timed roll passes straight through an attack.
entries.what_it_does: A roll that only moves the player is just a slow dash. Making it immune to damage turns it into a defensive tool: time it right and the attack goes through you. The cost is commitment. The roll has a fixed length and a cooldown, and a badly timed roll leaves you open.
entries.use_when: Action games with attacks meant to be dodged.
entries.watch_out: Immunity for the whole roll with no cooldown makes it a permanent shield. Add a cooldown or a vulnerable tail at the end.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives roll timings. 250 to 400 ms of roll with a cooldown of 200 to 400 ms are starting points. Infil's fighting game glossary describes invincible moves and notes that many games make backdashes briefly invincible.
entries.prompt:
Add a dodge roll with invincibility.
- On the dodge button: roll in the held direction (or facing) at 380 px/s for 300 ms.
- During the roll the player can't take damage.
- Another roll is allowed 250 ms after the previous one ends.
- Show the invincible part, for example by brightening the sprite.

Acceptance checks:
1. Rolling through a projectile takes no damage.
2. Getting hit right after the roll ends does damage.
3. Mashing can't chain rolls faster than one per 300 + 250 ms.

sources.title: Infil's Fighting Game Glossary: Invincible
Infil's Fighting Game Glossary: Backdash

entries.name: Aim assist
entries.summary: When the player fires roughly toward a target, send the shot at it if it is inside a small cone and in range.
entries.what_it_does: Aiming precisely with keys, a stick or a touch screen is hard, so many games quietly correct the shot. At fire time, look for targets inside a cone around the aim direction and within range, pick the one closest by angle, and fire at it. Halo calls this auto-aim or bullet magnetism. Doom's public source aims bullets this way: it looks for a target straight ahead, then a few degrees to each side, and sets the shot's vertical angle to hit it.
entries.use_when: Shooters with gamepad or touch input, and any game where the player can't aim freely, like this one, which only shoots left or right.
entries.watch_out: Too wide a cone feels like the game plays itself and can pick the wrong target when several are close. Competitive players notice it.
entries.starting_values: Doom checks about 5.6 degrees to each side (1<<26 in its angle units) before giving up. A cone of 5 to 15 degrees is a sensible starting range.
entries.prompt:
Add aim assist to shooting.
- When the player fires, find targets within 420 px whose direction is within 10 degrees of the aim direction.
- If there are any, fire at the one with the smallest angle difference. Otherwise fire straight.
- Only change the new shot's direction. Never move the player's aim or the camera.
- Make the cone and range settings, with a way to turn it off.

Acceptance checks:
1. Firing at a target slightly above or below the aim line hits it.
2. A target more than 10 degrees off is not hit unless aimed at.
3. With assist off, shots go exactly where aimed.

sources.title: DOOM source code, p_pspr.c (P_BulletSlope), id Software on GitHub
Halopedia: Aim assist
Using Aim Assistance to Balance First Person Shooters (Vicencio-Moreira, Mandryk, Gutwin, Bateman)

entries.name: Projectile leading
entries.summary: Enemies aim where the player will be when the shot arrives, not where they are now, so running in a straight line stops working.
entries.what_it_does: A turret that fires at the player's current position misses anyone who keeps moving. Leading estimates the travel time (distance divided by shot speed), predicts where the player will be after that time, recomputes the time to that point, and repeats a few times. Kain Shin's article walks through this iteration. A lead amount under 1 makes enemies less exact, which is often fairer.
entries.use_when: Turrets, bosses, and enemies with slow projectiles that should punish predictable movement.
entries.watch_out: Perfect leading against a player who can't change speed quickly is unfair. Lower the lead amount or the fire rate, and telegraph the shots.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives a fire rate or a lead amount. A few iterations are enough for straight shots, and a lead amount of 0.5 to 1 is a starting range.
entries.prompt:
Make the turret lead its shots.
- Shot speed 320 px/s.
- t = distance(turret, player) / shot speed. Repeat 4 times: predicted = player position + player velocity * t * 1; t = distance(turret, predicted) / shot speed.
- Fire toward the final predicted position.
- Use the player's current velocity only. Never read their input.

Acceptance checks:
1. Running in a straight line at constant speed gets hit.
2. Reversing right after a shot is fired dodges it.
3. A player standing still is hit the same as without leading.

sources.title: Predictive Aim Mathematics for AI Targeting (Kain Shin)

entries.name: Attack telegraph
entries.summary: Enemies show a clear wind-up before an attack becomes dangerous, so the player can react.
entries.what_it_does: An attack that is dangerous on the frame it starts can't be avoided by reacting, only by luck. A telegraph adds a visible wind-up (a pose, a color change, a marked danger zone) for a fixed time before the attack turns on. The wind-up has to be longer than reaction time plus the time the dodge needs.
entries.use_when: Every enemy attack the player is meant to dodge or block.
entries.watch_out: Keep tells consistent: the same wind-up always means the same attack. Very long tells make fights slow.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives one number. 300 to 600 ms of wind-up is a starting range; it has to cover reaction time plus the dodge.
entries.prompt:
Add telegraphs to enemy attacks.
- Before an attack becomes active, play a 450 ms wind-up: change the enemy's color or pose and mark the danger area.
- The attack can't deal damage during the wind-up.
- Use the same tell every time for the same attack.
- Randomize when attacks start, not how long the tell lasts.

Acceptance checks:
1. Every attack comes after a visible 450 ms wind-up.
2. A player who reacts to the tell can always avoid the attack.
3. No damage happens during the wind-up.

entries.name: Forgiving hitboxes
entries.summary: Make hazard hitboxes a little smaller than their art, so grazing a spike tip doesn't count.
entries.what_it_does: When the hitbox matches the art exactly, players get hurt by hits they are sure missed, especially on pointy shapes like spikes. Shrinking the damage box a few pixels inside the art, and the player's hurtbox a little inside their sprite, removes those near misses. Players rarely notice the gap, but they always notice getting hurt by one pixel.
entries.use_when: Hazards, enemy bodies, bullets: anything that hurts the player.
entries.watch_out: Don't shrink the player's own attacks against enemies. There, a slightly larger hitbox is the forgiving choice.
entries.starting_values: Game Maker's Toolkit notes that Celeste's spikes have a small hitbox, so touching the very tip doesn't kill you. Rodrigo Monteiro's guide says it's better for the player to dodge a hit they should have taken than to take one they shouldn't. 3 to 6 px of shrink at this size is a starting point.
entries.prompt:
Make damage hitboxes forgiving.
- Shrink each hazard's damage box by 5 px on each side compared to its art, a little more on the pointy top edge of spikes.
- Shrink the player's hurtbox about 2 px inside the sprite.
- Leave solid collision boxes unchanged. This only changes what hurts.
- Add a debug view that draws the damage boxes.

Acceptance checks:
1. Grazing a spike tip does no damage.
2. Landing squarely on spikes still hurts.
3. The player stands on solid ground exactly as before.

sources.title: Why Does Celeste Feel So Good to Play? (Game Maker's Toolkit)
The guide to implementing 2D platformers (Rodrigo Monteiro, Higher-Order Fun)

entries.name: Camera deadzone
entries.summary: The camera stays still while the player moves inside a window in the middle of the screen, and only scrolls when they push past its edge.
entries.what_it_does: A camera locked to the player moves every time they take a step, including small back-and-forth adjustments, and that constant motion is tiring to watch. A camera window lets the player move freely inside a box. When they push against an edge, the camera moves just enough to keep them inside. Itay Keren's camera talk traces this back to early arcade games and calls it a camera-window.
entries.use_when: Side-scrollers where the player makes lots of small moves.
entries.watch_out: A wide window shows less of what's ahead while running. Combine it with lookahead or keep it narrow.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives a size. A half-width of 40 to 100 px at this 640 px view is a starting point.
entries.prompt:
Add a camera window (deadzone) to horizontal follow.
- The window spans 80 px to each side of the screen center.
- If the player's center goes past the window's right edge, move the camera right by the overshoot. Same on the left.
- Inside the window the camera doesn't move.
- Clamp to the level bounds afterwards.

Acceptance checks:
1. Stepping back and forth within 80 px of center never moves the camera.
2. Running pushes the camera so the player stays at the window edge.
3. No jitter when the player stops at the edge.

sources.title: Scroll Back: The Theory and Practice of Cameras in Side-Scrollers (Itay Keren, GDC 2015 talk write-up)

entries.name: Camera platform snapping
entries.summary: The camera's height follows the player only when they land, so ordinary jumps don't bob the whole screen.
entries.what_it_does: A camera that follows the player vertically moves the whole world up and down on every jump. Platform snapping holds the vertical position while the player is in the air and eases to the new height after they land. Margins at the top and bottom still pull the camera if the player goes far enough. Itay Keren's camera talk credits Super Mario World with this.
entries.use_when: Platformers with a lot of jumping and vertical levels.
entries.watch_out: Long falls and very high jumps still need the top and bottom margins, or the player leaves the screen.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives numbers. Ease to the landing height with a speed of about 4 to 8 (exponential smoothing), and keep margins of about 40 px at the top and bottom of the screen.
entries.prompt:
Make the camera snap vertically to platforms.
- Keep a target camera height. Update it only while the player is on the ground: target = player's feet - 62% of the screen height.
- In the air, keep the target, unless the player gets within 40 px of the top or bottom of the screen. Then push the target to keep them on screen.
- Each frame: camera.y += (target - camera.y) * (1 - Math.exp(-6 * dt)).

Acceptance checks:
1. Jumping in place doesn't move the camera vertically.
2. Landing on a higher platform eases the camera up within about half a second.
3. A long fall still keeps the player on screen.

sources.title: Scroll Back: The Theory and Practice of Cameras in Side-Scrollers (Itay Keren, GDC 2015 talk write-up)

entries.name: Camera look-down
entries.summary: Holding down while standing still pans the camera down after a short delay, so the player can check a drop before taking it.
entries.what_it_does: Players hate jumping into a pit they can't see. Letting them hold down to peek uses an input they already have. A short delay keeps a quick tap of down from moving the camera. Itay Keren's camera talk points to Spelunky, where crouching or looking up shifts the camera, as a good use of controls already in the game.
entries.use_when: Levels with drops that go below the screen.
entries.watch_out: Don't pan while the player is moving, or it fights the normal follow.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives numbers. 100 to 150 px of pan after holding for about 300 ms is a starting point.
entries.prompt:
Add a look-down camera.
- While the player is on the ground, nearly still, and has held down for at least 300 ms, ease a camera offset to 120 px downward.
- Otherwise ease it back to 0.
- Ease with offset += (target - offset) * (1 - Math.exp(-6 * dt)).
- Clamp the camera to the level bounds.

Acceptance checks:
1. Holding down for 300 ms pans the view down by 120 px.
2. A quick tap of down doesn't move the camera.
3. Walking cancels the pan.

sources.title: Scroll Back: The Theory and Practice of Cameras in Side-Scrollers (Itay Keren, GDC 2015 talk write-up)

entries.name: Hit flash
entries.summary: Turn the target fully white for a few frames when it gets hit, so the player sees the hit land.
entries.what_it_does: In a busy scene it's hard to tell whether an attack connected. A short, solid white flash on the target is one of the clearest signals there is, and it reads even out of the corner of the eye. In the Juice it or lose it talk, the ball turns white every time it hits something.
entries.use_when: Any damage to enemies, and often to the player.
entries.watch_out: Long or repeated flashes can be a problem for photosensitive players. Keep them short and never flash the whole screen.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives a duration. 1 to 6 frames (about 17 to 100 ms) is a common starting range.
entries.prompt:
Add a hit flash.
- When an enemy takes damage, draw it solid white (a fill or a white shader, not a tint) for 70 ms (about 4 frames).
- Restart the timer on each new hit.
- Use real time.

Acceptance checks:
1. Each hit shows a solid white target.
2. The flash lasts about 70 ms at 30 and 144 fps.
3. Only the hit target flashes, never the full screen.

sources.title: Juice it or lose it (Jonasson and Purho talk)

entries.name: Damage numbers
entries.summary: Pop a number above the target on each hit showing the damage, then float it up and fade it out.
entries.what_it_does: Numbers tell the player how strong a hit was, which matters as soon as damage varies (critical hits, combos, upgrades). Spawn a small text at the hit point, move it up while slowing it down, and fade it near the end of its life. Offset each new number a little so quick hits don't stack on one spot, and make big hits bigger or a different color.
entries.use_when: RPGs, roguelikes, anything with damage that varies.
entries.watch_out: Games where a clean screen matters more, or where damage never changes. Too many numbers turn into noise.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives timings. 500 to 900 ms of life with a quick rise that slows down is a starting point.
entries.prompt:
Add floating damage numbers.
- On each hit, spawn a text with the damage at the top of the target, offset a few pixels sideways from the previous one.
- It rises at 90 px/s, slowing as it ages, and lives 700 ms. Fade it out over the last 200 ms.
- Bigger or critical hits use a larger font and a different color.
- Draw a dark outline or shadow so it reads on any background.

Acceptance checks:
1. Every hit shows its number once.
2. Quick hits don't stack numbers on the same pixel.
3. Numbers disappear after 700 ms.

entries.name: Jump squash and stretch
entries.summary: Stretch the character tall on takeoff and squash them wide on landing, scaled by how hard they land, then ease back.
entries.what_it_does: A rigid sprite that changes speed instantly looks stiff. A quick stretch on the jump frame and a squash on landing make the body read as moving with force. Scale from the feet so the character stays on the ground, ease back quickly, and leave the hitbox alone. Here it is driven by your own jumps and landing speed, not by a looping animation.
entries.use_when: Almost any character that jumps.
entries.watch_out: Never resize the collision box with the art, or the character snags on things.
entries.starting_values: Celeste's public player code sets the sprite scale to 0.6 by 1.4 on a jump, squashes up to 1.6 by 0.4 on landing depending on fall speed, and eases back toward 1 at 1.75 per second.
entries.prompt:
Add squash and stretch to the player sprite.
- On jump: scaleX = 1 - 0.4 * 0.75, scaleY = 1 + 0.4.
- On landing: s = min(fall speed / max fall speed, 1) * 0.4 * 1.5; scaleX = 1 + s, scaleY = 1 - s * 0.75.
- Every frame, move both scales toward 1 by 1.75 per second.
- Scale around the bottom center. Hitboxes stay unchanged.

Acceptance checks:
1. Jumping stretches the sprite and landing squashes it.
2. A big fall squashes more than a small hop.
3. The collision box never changes size.

sources.title: Celeste player source (Player.cs), public on GitHub
Why Does Celeste Feel So Good to Play? (Game Maker's Toolkit)
Juice it or lose it (Jonasson and Purho talk)

entries.name: Delayed damage bar
entries.summary: When health drops, a pale bar stays where the health was for a moment and then drains, showing how big the hit was.
entries.what_it_does: An instant drop in a health bar is easy to miss, and it doesn't show how much one hit took. Keeping a second, lighter bar at the old value for a short time and then draining it makes the size of the loss visible after the fact.
entries.use_when: Health bars, boss bars, shields.
entries.watch_out: Game logic and low-health warnings should read the real value, never the pale one.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives timings. Hold for 300 to 700 ms, then drain over a similar time, as a starting point.
entries.prompt:
Add a delayed damage bar behind the health bar.
- Keep ghostHealth. When health drops, leave ghostHealth where it was.
- 500 ms after the last hit, move ghostHealth toward health at 2 health points per second.
- When health goes up, set ghostHealth to it right away.
- Draw ghostHealth as a pale bar behind the real one.

Acceptance checks:
1. After a hit, the pale part shows the size of the loss for 500 ms.
2. Several quick hits extend the pale part instead of resetting it.
3. Healing never shows a pale part.

entries.name: Frame rate independence
aliases: game speed tied to frame rate
feels: too fast on a 144 Hz monitor
entries.summary: Run the game's physics in fixed steps of real time, so it plays at the same speed on a 60 Hz laptop and a 144 Hz monitor.
entries.what_it_does: Browsers and engines call your update once per screen refresh. If each call moves things a set amount, a 144 Hz screen runs the game 2.4 times faster than a 60 Hz one, and a slow frame makes it run slow. Multiplying by each frame's elapsed time fixes the speed, but the physics still comes out a little different at each frame rate, and a long frame can make it misbehave. The usual answer is a fixed timestep: add up the real elapsed time, run as many fixed-size updates as fit, and carry the remainder to the next frame. Glenn Fiedler's article "Fix Your Timestep!" walks through each approach. The demos on this site run this way, at 60 updates a second.
entries.use_when: Any game with physics, jumps or timing. Web games most of all, since players' screens run anywhere from 60 Hz to 240 Hz.
entries.watch_out: If an update takes longer than the time it covers, the game falls further behind every frame, so cap the elapsed time per frame. Drawing only the latest fixed step can look a little uneven on fast screens. Blend between the last two states to smooth it.
entries.starting_values: 60 updates a second is a common choice. Fiedler's example caps a frame's elapsed time at 0.25 seconds. The engine on this site runs 60 updates a second and caps a frame at 100 ms.
entries.prompt:
Make the game run at the same speed at any frame rate.
- Run game logic in fixed steps of 1/60 second, separate from drawing.
- Each frame, add the real elapsed time to an accumulator, run as many fixed steps as fit, and keep the remainder for the next frame.
- Cap the elapsed time per frame at 0.25 seconds so a stall doesn't trigger a burst of catch-up steps.
- Express every speed, gravity and timer per second and use the fixed step, never a per-frame amount.
- Draw once per screen frame. Optionally blend between the last two states for smooth motion.

Acceptance checks:
1. At 60 Hz and at 144 Hz, a 3 second run covers the same distance within 1 px.
2. Jump height and air time match at both rates.
3. With the CPU throttled 4x in dev tools, the frame rate drops but the game speed does not.

sources.title: Fix Your Timestep! (Glenn Fiedler, Gaffer On Games)
MDN: Window.requestAnimationFrame()

entries.name: Recoil
entries.summary: Push the player back a little every time they fire, so each shot has some force behind it.
entries.what_it_does: A shot that leaves the gun while nothing happens to the shooter feels like a toy. A short push opposite the aim direction on each shot makes the weapon feel strong, and with rapid fire the pushes add up, so firing nonstop has a cost. In his talk "The art of screenshake", Jan Willem Nijman of Vlambeer adds player knockback while shooting as one of the steps that turn a flat shooter into a punchy one, alongside screen shake and camera kick.
entries.use_when: Shooters, and any weapon that should feel heavy. Make it bigger for big guns and tiny or zero for fast, light ones.
entries.watch_out: Too much push throws off aim and can shove players into hazards or off ledges. Apply it as a velocity that wears off, not a jump in position, and keep it small where the platforming needs precision.
entries.starting_values: No checked source gives a number. Start with a push of 50 to 150 px/s per shot that wears off within about a tenth of a second, then tune it per weapon.
entries.prompt:
Add recoil to shooting.
- When the player fires, add 120 px/s of horizontal velocity opposite the aim direction.
- Let that extra velocity wear off at 1500 px/s² until it reaches zero, separate from normal movement.
- Stack the pushes from rapid fire, but cap the total so the player can't be launched.
- Run the push through normal collision so it never moves the player into a wall or hazard.
- Make the push size a per-weapon setting, with a way to turn it off.

Acceptance checks:
1. One shot moves the player back a few pixels, then they stop.
2. Firing five times quickly moves them back further, up to the cap.
3. Recoil never pushes the player through a wall.
4. With recoil off, shooting does not move the player.

sources.title: Jan Willem Nijman (Vlambeer), "The art of screenshake", INDIGO Classes 2013 (YouTube)

entries.name: Fast fall
entries.summary: Let the player press down while falling to drop at a higher, fixed speed, so they decide when to come down fast.
entries.what_it_does: Heavier fall gravity makes every jump come down faster. Fast fall leaves the jump alone and gives the player a button for it instead. In Super Smash Bros., tapping down on the stick while falling starts a fast fall: gravity is ignored and downward speed is set straight to the character's fast fall speed until they land, get hit or jump. Players use it to get back to the ground sooner and to vary their timing.
entries.use_when: Platformers and fighting games where players want control over their air time, especially with high or slow jumps.
entries.watch_out: Only start it while falling, not while rising, or it cuts jumps short by accident. Down may already mean drop through a platform or crouch, so decide which wins. Give it a sound or a visual cue so players know it happened.
entries.starting_values: SmashWiki's tables put most characters' fast fall speed at 1.4 times their normal fall speed in Brawl and 1.6 times in Smash 4.
entries.prompt:
Add fast fall.
- While the character is in the air and moving down, pressing down starts a fast fall.
- During a fast fall, ignore gravity and set the downward speed to 1.6 times the normal max fall speed.
- End the fast fall on landing, on a new jump, or when the character gets hit.
- Do nothing while the character is still rising.
- Play a short sound or flash when it starts.

Acceptance checks:
1. Pressing down after the peak makes the character land sooner. Log the air time both ways.
2. Pressing down while rising does not change the jump.
3. Fall speed during a fast fall is exactly 1.6 times the normal max fall speed.

sources.title: SmashWiki: Fast fall
